title: Ectopic pregnancy (tubal): diagnosis and management
subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
setting: Emergency department, early pregnancy unit, gynaecology ward, operating theatre
summary: Suspect ectopic pregnancy in any woman of reproductive age with pain, bleeding or collapse and a positive pregnancy test. Unstable: resuscitate and operate. Stable: transvaginal scan plus serial hCG; single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 for small unruptured ectopics with low hCG, surgery otherwise.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Symptoms: abdominal or pelvic pain, amenorrhoea, vaginal bleeding; also shoulder tip pain, dizziness or syncope, diarrhoea or other GI symptoms, urinary symptoms, rectal pressure or pain on defecation. Atypical presentation is common.
Signs: pelvic, adnexal or abdominal tenderness, cervical motion tenderness, peritonism, pallor, abdominal distension, pulse above 100/min or BP below 100/60 mmHg, shock or collapse.
Offer a urine pregnancy test to every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, bleeding, fainting or collapse, even when symptoms are non-specific or suggest gastroenteritis or UTI.

About a third of women with ectopic pregnancy have no risk factors. Known risks include previous ectopic, tubal surgery or sterilisation, pelvic inflammatory disease, assisted conception, and pregnancy with an IUCD in place.
In India, women often present late with rupture and haemoperitoneum; a pregnant woman in shock with free fluid is a ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise.

sections.title: Haemodynamically unstable or suspected rupture
items: Call the senior gynaecologist and anaesthetist; two large-bore IV cannulae; CBC, group and crossmatch, Rh typing, coagulation screen.
Resuscitate with warmed crystalloid and blood; activate the massive transfusion protocol if needed. Do not delay theatre for a formal scan or serum hCG.
Bedside ultrasound showing free fluid in a pregnant woman with shock supports immediate surgery.
Laparotomy when unstable or when laparoscopic skills or equipment are not available; salpingectomy is usual.

sections.title: Diagnosis in the stable woman (NICE NG126)
items: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS): an adnexal mass moving separately from the ovary containing a gestational sac with a yolk sac or fetal pole confirms tubal ectopic. An empty sac ('tubal ring'), complex adnexal mass, empty uterus or pseudo-sac, or moderate to large free fluid make ectopic probable or possible: interpret with hCG and the clinical picture. Always look for a heterotopic pregnancy.

Pregnancy of unknown location (PUL): treat as possible ectopic until the location is known. Take serum hCG twice, as close as possible to 48 hours apart (not earlier). Do not use hCG to locate the pregnancy.
hCG rise above 63% in 48 hours: likely intrauterine (ectopic not excluded); TVS in 7 to 14 days, earlier if hCG is 1500 IU/L or more.
hCG fall above 50%: pregnancy unlikely to continue; urine pregnancy test after 14 days and return if positive. Rise below 63% or fall below 50%: review in the early pregnancy unit within 24 hours.
Symptoms outweigh numbers: review promptly if pain or bleeding worsens, whatever the hCG. Do not use serum progesterone to diagnose location.
Before methotrexate: CBC, creatinine, liver enzymes, blood group and Rh.

sections.title: Choosing management (NICE NG126)
items: Surgery first-line if: significant pain, adnexal mass 35 mm or more, visible fetal heartbeat, serum hCG 5000 IU/L or more, or unable to return for follow-up.

Methotrexate first-line if ALL: no significant pain, unruptured ectopic with adnexal mass below 35 mm and no heartbeat, hCG below 1500 IU/L, no intrauterine pregnancy on scan, able to return. Give only when a viable intrauterine pregnancy has been excluded.
hCG 1500 to 4999 IU/L with the other methotrexate criteria: offer either methotrexate or surgery; methotrexate carries a higher chance of further intervention.

Expectant management: stable and pain free, mass below 35 mm, no heartbeat, hCG 1000 IU/L or less (consider up to 1500 IU/L), able to return. Repeat hCG on days 2, 4 and 7; if it falls 15% or more each time, then weekly until below 20 IU/L; otherwise senior review.

Surgery: laparoscopy when stable. Salpingectomy unless there are risk factors for infertility (such as a damaged contralateral tube), when salpingotomy is considered; up to 1 in 5 women need further treatment after salpingotomy.

sections.title: Single-dose methotrexate protocol
items: Methotrexate 50 mg/m2 body surface area IM once (day 1).

Serum hCG on days 4 and 7. If the fall between day 4 and day 7 is less than 15%, reassess and give a second dose (or proceed to surgery); then weekly hCG until negative. A rise between days 1 and 4 is common.

Contraindications: intrauterine pregnancy, breastfeeding, haemodynamic instability or signs of rupture, immunodeficiency, moderate to severe anaemia, leucopenia or thrombocytopenia, active pulmonary disease, active peptic ulcer, significant liver or kidney dysfunction, methotrexate hypersensitivity.

Advise: avoid folic acid supplements, NSAIDs, alcohol and strong sun until resolved; avoid intercourse and strenuous activity; expect some pain in the first week but return immediately for severe pain, dizziness or heavy bleeding; avoid conception for at least 3 months (ACOG, RCOG).

sections.title: Anti-D and follow-up
items: NICE 2026: do not give anti-D for ectopic pregnancy at up to 11+6 weeks. Offer anti-D at least 250 IU (50 mcg) IM to RhD-negative women at 12+0 to 12+6 weeks having medical or surgical management. Beyond this, follow routine anti-D guidance for sensitising events.
Earlier guidance (ACOG 2018; RCOG 2016 for surgically managed cases) gave anti-D more widely and many Indian units still do; follow a written unit policy.
After salpingectomy: urine pregnancy test at 3 weeks. After salpingotomy: serum hCG at 7 days, then weekly until negative.
Non-tubal ectopics (caesarean scar, cervical, interstitial or cornual, ovarian, abdominal) and heterotopic pregnancy need senior or specialist management.
Advise early self-referral for a transvaginal scan in any future pregnancy.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Not doing a pregnancy test in a woman with abdominal pain, diarrhoea or syncope; excluding ectopic because there are no risk factors.
Diagnosing complete miscarriage on an empty uterus without a previous scan-confirmed intrauterine pregnancy: manage as PUL.
Giving methotrexate before a viable intrauterine pregnancy is excluded, or co-prescribing folic acid or NSAIDs with methotrexate.
Discharging PUL without a 48-hour hCG plan and clear safety-net advice.
Waiting for scan or hCG results in a woman who is shocked.

drugs.name: Methotrexate
drugs.dose: 50 mg/m2 IM single dose; second dose if hCG falls less than 15% between day 4 and day 7
drugs.notes: Check CBC, creatinine and liver enzymes first. Avoid folic acid, NSAIDs and alcohol. Avoid conception for at least 3 months.

drugs.name: Anti-D immunoglobulin
drugs.dose: At least 250 IU (50 mcg) IM within 72 hours
drugs.notes: NICE 2026: RhD-negative women at 12+0 to 12+6 weeks having medical or surgical management; not needed up to 11+6 weeks.

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 1 g orally or IV every 6 hours; maximum 4 g/day (3 g/day if weight below 50 kg or liver disease)
drugs.notes: Preferred analgesic after methotrexate; avoid NSAIDs.
